MY MUSICAL
ARCHIVE

Music is the source of much of my drive, whether that's general success, creative inspiration, or just energy. It's one of my favorite human experiences, and a big part of what allows me to climb new peaks. That's why this whole site plays like a score.

If I had to sum up eight years of listening in one word, it's more. This dashboard tracks the shifts, the deep dives, and the daily habits behind that word, all pulled straight from eight years of Apple Music data.

      1. All-Time Consumption Overview & Macro-Genre Taxonomy

      This is the all-time genre split. Trap/Hip-Hop, the combined Classical family, and IDM/Electronic take about three-quarters of my 3,398 logged hours between them. Trap and classical sit on opposite ends of that spread, but they've never felt like opposites to me. Hip-hop is what first made me feel something specific about music, Kanye and Travis had me wanting to be great. Classical came later, and it does the exact same thing now: a good bar and a Haydn quartet give me the same chill.

      Macro-Genre Duration Share (%)

      Outer ring: Baroque, Classical, Romantic and 20th Century collapsed into one combined Classical slice (561.2 hrs, 16.5% of all-time listening) alongside the other macro genres. Inner ring: the same four shown as four adjacent slices. Trap/Hip-Hop remains the largest single category at 42.9%.

      Before & After Sept 2025 — The Classical Pivot in Two Numbers

      Split at the real inflection point (Sept 2025). All figures below are aggregated directly from the validated monthly genre series.

      The story behind the pivot

      September 2025. A coworker who always had headphones on when he wasn't working, I always try to put people onto Aphex Twin first. He already knew him, so I pushed harder, offered him $5 to sit through a brutal six-minute track. He said keep your $5 and sent me something back instead: Scriabin's “The Poem of Ecstasy.” I gave it the same attention I give a hidden Aphex track, eyes closed, room blocked out, and that was it, I wanted more. He fed me a few recommendations, then I took it from there on my own, chronologically: Bach, Mozart, Haydn, stuck on Beethoven for a while before I finally got why he's a household name. I don't work with the guy anymore, but I still owe him that one song.

      Monthly Ledger

      Complete month-by-month record of listening hours, top genre, top artist/composer, and friction rates. Top Artist/Composer aggregates every performance of a composer's work; hover any artist to see the Top Performer, the credited artist ranked exactly as Apple Replay does. They legitimately differ, Oct 2025 is J.S. Bach by composer (758 min across many performers) but Aphex Twin by performer (592 min), which is what Replay shows. Top Album is ranked independently of both, and this ledger doubles as an archive of my favorite albums: if something hit the top of a month, it's because I genuinely loved it.

      3. How I Listen — Behavior, Binge Days & Listening Clock

      This is where the project turned into a bit of a mirror, small, specific facts about myself I didn't actually know until I built this. Merged view of my listening behavior, extreme days, and the weekly rhythm of when I actually listen, rebuilt across the full archive. Late-night listening (8pm–4am) climbed steadily across three of the four eras, from 31.5% up to a peak of 41.7%, then eased back down to 36.9% in the current one. Daytime (8am–4pm) moved the opposite direction: 37.9% down to a low of 26.2%, then back up to 32.9% now. That peak was college, late nights built into the schedule, and my listening's gotten a little more daytime since I graduated. Daily mean is 1.47 hrs (std dev 1.56); the highest real day is 5.80σ above the mean, and no day exceeds 6σ.

      Your Listening Clock (Austin, TX — Central Time)

      Counter-intuitive

      The Skip Paradox

      Baroque gets skipped 56.8% of the time. Classical, 49.5%. Trap/Hip-Hop — the genre I actually grew up on — sits at 45.5%. Statistically, I am just as likely to browse and skip through Bach as I am through Travis Scott. I don't feel obligated to sit through a full piece after the first couple of listens, doesn't matter if it's Bach. First time through, sure, start to finish. After that, it's the parts that hit hardest that I go back for.

      Real skip rates run 41.5–66.3% across every genre (Rock lowest, the residual Other bucket highest) — no genre earns dramatically more "focused" listening than any other. The reverence I think I bring to classical music doesn't show up in how I actually listen to it: median skip point is 0.8% into the track, same restless habit regardless of what's playing.

      How I Listen — Playback Source by Era

      Where each play started, from Play Activity’s Feature Name field. The Apple Classical App didn’t exist before 2025 — it now accounts for essentially all of the growth in that era.

      Saved-album listening fell from 57% (2018-20) to 10% (2025-26) as playlists, search, and eventually the Classical app took over as entry points. The social/"For You" layer of Apple Music went from 0.7% of plays to exactly 0% and has stayed there since 2021.

      Discovery Ratio Trajectory (%) — real

      Real ratio (% of plays that are a track's first-ever play): rose gradually from 5.4% (2018-19) to 9.7% (2026) — a real but gentle upward drift, not a spike-and-normalize pattern. (Recomputed as a share of individual plays, not distinct track-days — an earlier pass overstated this by roughly 2x.)

      My Anchor

      Aphex Twin is the bridge across all the genres here. Calling what he does a genre feels like it undersells it, sedative tracks like #3 sit right next to something as abrasive as Ziggomatic 17, and both are fully him. What's kept me coming back for years is that there's always more to find: a whole SoundCloud dump I didn't discover until two years in, tracks released under aliases I only unearthed after I thought I'd finished his “main” discography. He doesn't get old because he never runs out of range.
